intro: This unit names four kinds of play and the rooms they need. Soccer uses a pitch. Basketball began in a gym in 1891. Races use a track. Swimming uses a measured pool. Ice hockey uses a rink.

Then the unit looks at turns you can see. A referee's whistle, a starting line, eleven soccer players, and five basketball players all come from written rules. The IHSA, begun in 1900, is Illinois's school-sport room.
bigQuestion: How do places and written rules help children share a game?

write.prompt: Pick two places from this unit (pitch, gym, track, pool, or rink). For each, write one true fact from the reading: a name, a date, or a number.
tips: Use a fact from the lesson, not a guess.
Name the place in one word.
Add a date or a measurement.
Do not write how to play the sport.

title: Play Has Kinds

chapters.title: Balls, Races, Water, Ice
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do ball games, races, swimming, and ice games need different places?

story.title: Four Doors in One School
story.kicker: A class walks past a gym, a field, a pool door, and a cold rink poster.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz takes her class down the school hall. First they peek in the gym. The floor is wood. Two hoops hang at the ends. A red ball sits in a bin.
Next they look out at the grass. White lines make a big rectangle. "That grass is for soccer," she says. "The rectangle is called a pitch."
They pass a door with a picture of water. A sign says Pool. Another poster shows ice skates. "Water and ice need their own rooms," she says. "A field cannot hold them."
Back in class she writes four words: ball, race, water, ice. "Each kind of play has a place. Today we learn the names of those places."
story.think: Which of the four doors is most like a place near your school?

lessons.title: A Soccer Pitch
lessons.mainIdea: Association football, called soccer in the United States, is played on a grass or turf rectangle called a pitch.
reading: In 1863, clubs in London wrote shared rules for a kicking game. They formed the Football Association. People in the United States often call that game *soccer*.
The field is a *pitch*. It is a long rectangle of grass or turf. Two goals stand at the ends. The ball must stay inside the lines most of the time.

words.d: the kicking game whose rules were written in London in 1863
the rectangle of grass or turf used for soccer

look.title: The 1863 meeting
look.text: On 26 October 1863, football clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and began the Football Association, so different towns could use the same kicking rules.
look.cite: The Football Association, founding meeting, London, 26 October 1863 (standard history of association football)
look.prompt: Why did clubs from different towns need one set of rules?

check.q: When did London clubs form the Football Association?
check.why: The Football Association began in London in 1863.

check.q: What is the soccer field called?
check.why: The reading calls the rectangle a pitch.

check.q: What stands at the ends of a pitch?
check.why: Two goals stand at the ends of the pitch.

lessons.title: A Gym and a Hoop
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball began in 1891 in a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, when James Naismith hung peach baskets.
reading: In December 1891, *James Naismith* taught in Springfield, Massachusetts. Winter kept his class inside. He needed a game that fit a gym.
He hung peach *baskets* on the balcony. Players threw a soccer ball toward the baskets. That indoor game became basketball.

words.d: the teacher who invented basketball in 1891
the peach basket, and later the hoop, that players throw toward

look.title: Naismith's winter problem
look.text: Naismith wrote that he needed an indoor game for a class at the International YMCA Training School in Springfield in December 1891. He used a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941); Basketball Hall of Fame, Springfield, Massachusetts
look.prompt: Why did Naismith invent a game for a gym instead of a field?

check.q: In what year did Naismith hang the peach baskets?
check.why: The reading dates the gym game to December 1891.

check.q: Where was Naismith teaching?
check.why: He taught in Springfield, Massachusetts.

check.q: What did he hang on the balcony?
check.why: He hung peach baskets for the new indoor game.

lessons.title: A Track Is 400 Meters
lessons.mainIdea: A standard outdoor running track is 400 meters around in the inside lane.
reading: A running *track* is an oval path. Runners stay in lanes. The inside lane of a standard outdoor track is 400 meters around.
World Athletics is the group that writes many track rules. School tracks in the United States often use that same 400-meter size so times can be compared.

words.d: an oval path with lanes for running races
a marked strip a runner stays in during a race

look.title: One lap on a standard outdoor track
look.cite: World Athletics Technical Rules, standard outdoor running track length

check.q: How long is one lap in the inside lane outdoors?
check.why: A standard outdoor track is 400 meters around in the inside lane.

check.q: What is a lane?
choices: a marked strip for one runner
check.why: A lane is the marked strip a runner stays in.

check.q: Who writes many international track rules?
check.why: The reading names World Athletics.

lessons.title: Races in Ancient Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: The ancient Olympic Games in Greece included running races in a stadium.
reading: Long ago, people ran races at *Olympia* in Greece. Those games are called the ancient Olympic Games. A main race was a sprint down a stadium.
The stadium was a long dirt path, not a modern 400-meter oval. Still, it was a place built for a race. A race needs a path people can see.

words.d: the place in Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held

look.title: Two race paths
look.text: Look at a long straight dirt stadium in old Olympia. Then look at a modern oval track with eight painted lanes. Both are paths built so a race has a place.
look.prompt: What is the same about the two paths? What is different?

check.q: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?
check.why: The reading places those games at Olympia in Greece.

check.q: What kind of place was the old stadium?
choices: a long dirt path for a race
check.why: It was a long dirt path, not a modern oval.

check.q: What does a race need, in this lesson?
check.why: A race needs a visible path.

lessons.title: A Pool Has a Measured Length
lessons.mainIdea: Many United States school pools are 25 yards long so swim times can be compared.
reading: A swimming *pool* is a tank built to hold water. The length is measured. Many school and club pools in the United States are 25 yards long.
Swimmers race from one wall to the other. A 25-yard pool is called short course yards. Longer pools of 50 meters are used in many world meets.

words.d: a tank built to hold water for swimming
a unit of length; many U.S. school pools are 25 yards long

look.title: Common race-pool lengths
look.cite: USA Swimming and NFHS swimming: 25-yard short course is common in U.S. schools; FINA/World Aquatics Olympic pool is 50 meters
look.prompt: Which number is a common U.S. school pool length in yards?

check.q: How long are many U.S. school pools?
check.why: The reading says many school pools are 25 yards long.

check.q: What is a pool in this lesson?
choices: a tank built to hold water
check.why: A pool is a tank built to hold water.

check.q: How long is an Olympic-size pool?
check.why: The reading says many world meets use 50-meter pools.

lessons.title: Ice Needs a Rink
lessons.mainIdea: Ice hockey in North America is played on a rink about 200 feet long.
reading: Ice hockey needs frozen water. That place is a *rink*. In North America a National Hockey League rink is about 200 feet long and 85 feet wide.
A dry gym floor cannot hold that ice. A grass pitch cannot hold it either. Ice play needs a cold room made for ice.

words.d: the ice floor used for hockey and some skating games

look.title: An NHL ice rink
look.cite: National Hockey League rink dimensions, 200 by 85 feet
look.prompt: How long is the hockey rink in feet?

check.q: About how long is an NHL rink?
check.why: The reading gives 200 feet as the length.

check.q: What is a rink?
check.why: A rink is the ice floor.

check.q: Why can't a grass pitch hold hockey ice?
choices: ice needs a cold room made for ice
check.why: Ice play needs a cold room. Grass cannot hold the ice.

chapters.title: A Turn Everyone Can See
chapters.bigQuestion: How do a whistle, a line, and a team size help people take fair turns?

story.title: The Whistle and the Line
story.kicker: A starter lifts a whistle. Shoes wait behind a white line.
paragraphs: On field day the starter stands beside a white line. Runners curl their toes behind it. No one may step over until the sound.
The starter blows a *whistle*. Eight children run. Eight more wait for the next heat. The wait is part of the race, not a punishment.
Later, in the gym, a soccer game uses another rule from the Laws of the Game. Each side may put eleven players on the pitch. Extra children wait as substitutes.
Ms. Ortiz says, "A turn you can see needs a mark and a signal. A team has a size written in a book, not just a feeling."
story.think: When did you wait so someone else could go first?

lessons.title: A Whistle Starts Many Games
lessons.mainIdea: Referees in soccer and basketball use a whistle so the whole room hears the same start or stop.
reading: In soccer, the referee carries a *whistle*. The Laws of the Game say the referee starts and stops play. The sound is for everyone on the pitch, not just one player.
Basketball officials use a whistle too. When the whistle blows, players are supposed to stop. One sound can reach a noisy gym.

words.d: a tool that makes a sharp sound to start or stop play
the official who starts and stops a soccer match

look.title: Who starts soccer play
look.text: The Laws of the Game give the referee power to start and stop play and to use a whistle so players and fans hear the same decision.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 5 (The Referee), current public summary of the referee's duties
look.prompt: Why does one person hold the whistle instead of every player?

check.q: Who starts and stops a soccer match?
check.why: The Laws of the Game give that job to the referee.

check.q: Why use a whistle in a gym?
choices: one sound can reach a noisy room
check.why: The reading says one sound can reach a noisy gym.

check.q: What should basketball players do when the whistle blows?
check.why: Officials use the whistle so players stop.

lessons.title: A Line You Must Not Cross Yet
lessons.mainIdea: Runners start from behind a line so every racer begins from the same place.
reading: On a track, runners wait behind a starting *line*. If someone steps over early, that is a false start. The race is not fair yet.
World Athletics races use starting blocks in many sprint events. The blocks hold the feet. The line still marks where the race begins.

words.d: the mark that shows where a race or turn begins
leaving before the start signal

look.title: Toes behind the line
look.text: Look at eight pairs of shoes behind a white line. One shoe creeps over the paint. The starter raises a hand. That runner has left too soon.
look.prompt: Why does one early step make the race unfair?

check.q: Where do track runners wait?
check.why: They wait behind the starting line.

check.q: What is a false start?
check.why: A false start is leaving before the signal.

check.q: What do many sprint races use to hold the feet?
check.why: The reading names starting blocks.

lessons.title: Eleven on a Soccer Side
lessons.mainIdea: The Laws of the Game allow eleven players on each soccer team on the pitch.
reading: Soccer has a written team size. The Laws of the Game say each team may have eleven players on the *pitch*. One of them is the goalkeeper.
If more than eleven play at once, the extra person is not allowed. Substitutes wait off the pitch until a referee lets a change happen.

words.d: the rectangle where soccer is played
the player allowed to use the hands in the penalty area

look.title: Players on the pitch
rows: goalkeepers on the pitch at once
look.cite: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 3 (The Players): eleven players per team
look.prompt: How many players may one side have on the pitch?

check.q: How many soccer players may one team have on the pitch?
check.why: Law 3 allows eleven per team, including the goalkeeper.

check.q: Who may use the hands in the penalty area?
check.why: The reading names the goalkeeper.

check.q: Where do extra players wait?
check.why: Substitutes wait off the pitch.

lessons.title: Five on a Basketball Side
lessons.mainIdea: A basketball team may have five players on the court at one time.
reading: Basketball uses a different number. Officials allow five players per team on the *court*. That number is in the playing rules, not just a habit.
Naismith's first game in 1891 used nine players on a side because his class was large. Later rules settled on five. Team size is written. It can change when a rule book changes.

words.d: the marked floor used for basketball

look.title: From nine to five
look.text: Naismith's first class in 1891 had eighteen students, so he used nine on a side. Later amateur and school rules set five players on the court for each team.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941); NFHS / NCAA basketball rules on five players per team
look.prompt: What changed: the gym, or the written number?

check.q: How many basketball players may one team have on the court now?
check.why: Current playing rules allow five on the court.

check.q: How many were on a side in Naismith's first class game?
check.why: Eighteen students made nine on a side.

check.q: What can change a team size?
check.why: The reading says team size is written and can change with the book.

lessons.title: Both Sides Use the Same Words
lessons.mainIdea: Fair play means both sides hear and use the same written rule.
reading: A *fair* start uses one line and one signal for every racer. A fair soccer match uses the same Laws of the Game for both clubs.
If only one team knew the offside rule, the match would not be shared. Sharing a game means sharing the words in the book.

words.d: using the same rule for each side

look.title: One book, two sides
look.text: Two teams walk onto a pitch. The referee carries one rule book. Both captains hear the same start. No team gets a private whistle.
look.prompt: What would go wrong if each team used a different book?

check.q: What does fair mean here?
choices: using the same rule for each side
check.why: Fair means the same rule for each side.

check.q: What do both soccer clubs use?
choices: the same Laws of the Game
check.why: Both sides use the same Laws of the Game.

check.q: Sharing a game means sharing
check.why: The reading says sharing the words in the book.

lessons.title: Illinois Schools Use Shared Rules Too
lessons.mainIdea: The Illinois High School Association writes rules so schools in one state can meet.
reading: The *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA, began in 1900. It runs state meets so schools can use shared rules.
IHSA boys wrestling state champions were first named in 1937. Those dates belong to school sport. They do not invent running or wrestling. They mark a state room.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, begun in 1900

look.title: A state meet date
look.text: The IHSA lists 1937 as the first year of a boys wrestling state championship. The association itself dates to 1900.
look.cite: Illinois High School Association records: IHSA founded 1900; boys wrestling state championship 1937
look.prompt: Which date marks the association, and which date marks one sport's state meet?

check.q: When did the IHSA begin?
check.why: The IHSA began in 1900.

check.q: When were the first IHSA boys wrestling state champions named?
check.why: IHSA records list 1937.

check.q: What do those dates mark?
check.why: They mark Illinois school sport, not the invention of the games.

review.why: The referee holds that job under the Laws of the Game.
Leaving early is a false start.
